The House resumed from Tuesday, April 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-19, to amend the Canada Pension Plan, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I had the opportunity of commencing my intervention in this debate. The introduction was somewhat extended because of certain interjections from across the way. It was not my intention to be so controversial. Nevertheless, I will heed the interjection attributed to the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) and get to the bill.
We are discussing today a bill that will remove some of the inequities and inadequacies of the Canada Pension
Canada Pension Plan
Plan. To the extent this objective is being attained, we welcome the bill.
The detailed notes on the bill to amend the Canada Pension Plan, attached to the news release announcing the introduction of Bill C-19 on April 5, 1974, state as one of its main provisions the equal treatment of male and female contributors and beneficiaries. I quote:
The bill amends the present provisions of the Canada Pension Plan so the surviving spouses and children of a deceased or disabled female contributor will qualify for benefits under the same conditions as surviving spouses and children of a male contributor.
As the technique to achieve this change involves only the deletion of all references to "widowers" and the substitution of "survivor's pensions", it seems incomprehensible that this provision was not incorporated in the initial legislation. Perhaps the public demand was a contributing factor in the decision to make this essential and logical change.
The Royal Commission on the Status of Women was appointed in 1967, and its terms of reference were:
To inquire into and report upon the status of women in Canada and to recommend what steps might be taken by the federal government to ensure for women equal opportunities with men in all aspects of Canadian society.
With respect to the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan, two amendments were proposed by the commission. The first recommended an extension to the husband and children of a female contributor of the provisions presently applicable to the wife and children of a male contributor. In this connection I should like to refer to a document presented to the recent annual meeting of the Progressive Conservative party. On page 3 of that document, in section 19, the following appears:
The Report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women refers to the fact there are sex differences within the terms of reference of the Canada Pension Plan and recommends that they be removed. Although contributions are equal, regardless of sex or marital status, there are differences in the benefits derived from this source by the dependent or survivor. In this day of shared responsibilities the loss of the income of the female would create as great a hardship as would the loss of the income of the male. Survivor's benefits should be provided for both male and female contributors on a like basis.
The second proposed amendment recommended by the commission was that provision be made for the participation in these plans of the spouse remaining at home. On October 30, 1973, I believed I was voicing the views of many hon. members, some of whom had already so expressed themselves, when I stated, as reported on page 7373 of Hansard of that day:
There is a general oversight in the Canada Pension Plan as it relates to housewives. I know I am not the first member to bring this matter to the attention of the House; others who have preceded me have done so. But I think it is a matter of real concern which should be taken under advisement and dealt with favourably.
It w'ould probably be more correct to say that the Canada Pension Plan does not relate to housewives, and this is why I say it is an oversight. I feel, and I am sure many in my party feel, that the government should devise some mechanism whereby housewives could contribute to the Canada Pension plan and benefit upon retirement or upon reaching retirement age. Of course, there is some question whether a housewife ever retires. In the event of the death of a husband, a housewife could then receive a more adequate income.

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
This has to do with the possibility of bringing housewives-other terms are used for them now in connection with this particular matter-within the scope of the plan. I should like again to refer to the background paper from which I have previously quoted:
The assumption that the female is always the spouse who remains at home to tend the "home fires" is not currently valid. Therefore, since the spouse who works at home does in fact contribute to the family support by providing goods and services which are invaluable to the family unit, Progressive Conservatives believe this person should share in the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan just as does the partner who is actually registered as being gainfully employed. Amendments will be made to the Canada Pension Plan to give effect to this policy.
I should like to refer in this connection also to the presentation made by the National Farmers Union in 1973 with reference to the position of farm wives. It deals with the same subject but looks at it from the point of view of the lady of the house in the agricultural industry. I will quote one brief section as follows:
Many farm women work as partners with their husbands in performing the duties of farming. The decision whether or not the farming unit wishes to pay an additional annual premium to provide a farm wife with future Canada Pension Plan benefits should be made optional. We request that the necessary amendments to the Canada Pension Plan be effected.
Now I should like to refer to the statement made by the minister in his discussion paper "Housewives and the Canada Pension Plan". I appreciated the view taken by the minister when he stated:
The housewife who remains at home is just as much a producer of goods and services as the paid worker, and in our view she should also have the opportunity to provide for a more financially secure future. Canada has given some of its workers an opportunity to do this through the Canada and the Quebec Pension Plans. To neglect to do the same for some three and one half million other workers in the home is to ignore the essential nature of their work.
In my speech of last October 30, from which I quoted a few minutes ago, I stressed this important aspect. We certainly appreciate the fact that in acting on all these recommendations the government has seen fit to move forward. I believe the minister is sincerely convinced that this is a valid position to take. We appreciate what has been done.
I should also like to read the statement which appears at the bottom of page 2 of the document "Housewives and the Canada Pension Plan", to which I have referred. The minister stated:
For all these reasons, provision must be made for the participation of housewives in the Canada or the Quebec Pension Plan. A comprehensive study will be required to determined the best way of achieving this. Two approaches seem to have considerable merit:
(i)	crediting to the spouse remaining at home a portion of the
contributions of the employed spouse and those contributions made
by the employer on the employed spouse's behalf, and
(ii)	on an optional basis, permitting the spouse at home to contribute
as a self-employed worker.
Each of these proposals has to be weighed to determine its relative advantages or disadvantages, but on the face of it it appears, as the minister says, that both have considerable merit. We on this side of the House are pleased to see the government prepared to adopt the measures we have been advocating, either in this bill or in future legislation. Whatever the pressures, and from whatever their source, this is another step in the direction of making this con-

tributory and portable plan better able to meet the needs of Canadians today.
Another amending provision is that which provides for an escalation in the yearly maximum pensionable earnings by 1214 per cent each year until they catch up to the industrial composite. The decision to make this amendment applicable for the years after 1975 perpetuates, in my view, a somewhat unjust situation. With inflation increasing at the rate of approximately 10 per cent per year, it seems to me that providing for at least full escalation at this time would be to the benefit of the workers of the country. The maximum benefits are meagre enough, without delaying the opportunity of contributing a higher premium to ensure more adequate benefits. The levels are $6,600 in 1974 and $7,400 in 1975, as outlined in Bill C-224 passed last session. I stated then, and I state again now, that those levels are not high enough for 1974 and 1975.
The proposed amendment which would reduce the qualifying level for contributions in any given year from 12 per cent to 10 per cent of the year's maximum pensionable earnings-it would, for 1975, reduce it from $800, as presently established, to $700-is very desirable, as is the intent to delete the present special requirement under which self-employed persons must earn at least 1 lA of the year's basic earnings to qualify as contributors in any year.
It seems to me we must make an attempt to permit every working Canadian to participate in this plan regardless of income. To the extent that these changes will provide greater opportunity for people at lower income levels to participate in the Canada Pension Plan, and in particular increased numbers of fishermen, farmers and other self-employed persons, we commend the minister for his efforts.
The Canada Pension Plan is a contributory plan, and as such I have never felt the government had any right to penalize individuals for whatever they earn after they have retired from regular employment. I agree with those who feel we should encourage people to retire at the usual retirement age. However, life is difficult enough for people of that age without our complicating things more for them by imposing an extra hardship on them when they try to earn a little extra money to help make ends meet.
I am, therefore, pleased to see the proposal in this bill to drop the earnings test for those aged 65 and over. When I spoke on this subject in October I stated I would favour the complete elimination of the earnings test for pensioners aged 65 and over. I made references at that time to a number of letters I had received from pensioners in very difficult straits who were being penalized for earning more than $960 a year. I am sure these people are pleased to see the government has now come round to the point of making this very desirable change.
The last point I would like to make is one that has been made by members from this party on many occasions, and that is that the government should lower the age of retirement for guaranteed income supplement, old age security and Canada Pension Plan purposes to age 60, beginning with an immediate reduction to age 64 and with a yearly reduction thereafter to age 60. As I have said, this sugges-
April 17, 1974

tion has been made many times previously, but we just want to remind the minister once again in the hope that he will give very close study and attention to this area. If he does I am sure he will receive the appreciation of a great many citizens of this country.
In conclusion, I commend the minister for the action that he has taken in this bill and assure him that he has my support for these measures. I urge him, however, to continue to heed the many requests from this side of the House, and from the people of Canada, regarding those other matters that will make the Canada Pension Plan more effective and responsive to the needs of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak in this debate. I listened with interest during the question period when the House leader for the government party explained the absence of four senior economics ministers. When he came to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), he said that he had gotten a bill through the House this week so consequently had the day off. I presume that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is looking forward to a well deserved day off as soon as we get this bill through the House. There may, of course, be some other bill that he has in mind, and he may be looking to get two days off at once. If so, he can go down to Florida and watch the Dolphins in their spring training. In any case, I am glad the minister is here today and I hope he enjoys whatever time off the House leader gives him on completion of this bill.
The minister has brought forth a very complicated bill. On first reading it I was more perplexed than I was enlightened. One thing I noticed missing was the cost. I do not want to make this any part of the thrust of my speech, but when one buys things in this world one should know what they cost. I am willing to buy this bill, and I am pleased to buy it, but I should like to know what it costs as well. In all of the publicity I have seen and read-and believe me, Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of it in connection with this bill-I have seen no sign of increased contributions on the part of anyone.
There is a story going around the Hill, probably apocryphal, that when the minister introduced the increased family allowances he was asked by a reporter how much it would cost, and he replied that nobody had stopped to work it out.
I can hardly believe that that was the case, but in any event I did come across the cost of this Canada Pension Plan increase in an article by John G. Doherty of the Financial Times. In talking of pension costs he said that the costs assume a 4 per cent rate of inflation. He went on to say:
The employer's contributions will have to be increased in three different ways. First of all, the company must raise its contributions to cover pension benefits currently being earned by its existing employees.
Secondly, the employer must face the fact that his previous contributions for pension rights earned in the past by his current workers made no allowance for escalating benefits. Refunding for this will cost about $16 million.
The employer must also refund another $5 million to cover the cost of increased benefits to existing pensioners.
Canada Pension Plan
All together, the refunding will raise payroll costs by an additional 7.5 per cent a year if the refunding is amortized over 16 years. Thus, the total annual increase in payroll cost will rise by 11.8 per cent considering an assumed rise of only 4 per cent in the cost of living.
I put that on the record simply to balance things off, and to indicate to the people of Canada that they will not get anything for nothing in this world. The government may like to pretend that this money is coming out of its pockets, that it is simply being generous, but in truth it comes out of the recipients' pockets sooner or later. I think this should be part of an open government policy, and I would have increased my admiration for the minister and his staff had he seen fit to do this when he put out all the other publicity kits that heralded this bill.
I should now like to talk about the pensions of servicemen. Servicemen in the armed forces are required to pay into the Canadian Forces Superannuation Fund, from which they draw their pension. They also pay into the Canada Pension Plan which has been integrated with Canadian forces superannuation. I might say that this has created just about as much discussion and unhappiness in the forces as that other integration we sometimes hear about. In any case, the two pensions are now integrated. They are not, however, stacked.
When a serviceman draws his Canada Pension Plan benefit, if he does eventually qualify for it, his CFSA cheque is reduced by part of the amount of the CPP benefit. This is not generally known, and it does create a great deal of unhappiness among servicemen who are unable to see why part of their pension deduction goes to the Canada Pension Plan which is of little or no benefit to them.
Many servicemen suspect that the CFSA fund is very large and perhaps is being used to give body to the CPP fund. In any case, they see no reason or advantage in paying into the fund, from which they will not receive the same material benefit as other contributors. Government employees of all kinds have always wanted open disclosure of the state of their pension funds, but this disclosure seems extremely difficult to get.
Mr. Geoff Johnson pointed this out in an article the other day on disability pensions awarded under the Canada Pension Plan. He said:
Suppose, as a former contributor to the Canadian Forces Superannuation Account who is not yet 65, you are now receiving military superannuation.
And suppose that you become entitled to a disability pension under the Canadian or Quebec Pension Plans.
The article continued:
If you are entitled to a disability pension your annuity under the provisions of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act will be reduced accordingly.
Later in the article it was stated:
The reduction takes effect from the date you received the disability pension-and the National Defence Headquarters suggests you let them know right away to "avoid an over-payment of your annuity which would have to be recovered."
What kind of help is this to a disabled person?

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
Why give him the disability pension in the first place?
Why create all that bookkeeping to achieve precisely nothing?
Those are the kind of difficulties bureaucrats get themselves into when they attempt to look after every possible contingency.
I respectfully suggest that there are several anomalies in Bill C-19 which may cause just as much trouble indeed as exists under the act.
I will not bother you with all the details of the case I have before me, but a constituent of mine who wrote me found that when he was on superannuation, having been employed by HMC Dockyard and retired, and he eventually came to get the Canada Pension Plan they immediately started deducting $18.49 a month from his superannuation pension. It is extremely difficult for these people to understand this bureaucratic jungle talk that goes on in letters of explanation sent back to them. I would only ask you to bear in mind that this is just one sentence from a letter which was supposed to solve this man's predicament. The letter states:
When the Canada Pension Plan came into effect on January 1, 1966, it was decided that in order to avoid increasing the pension deductions of persons required to contribute under the Public Service Superannuation Act, the amount which a public servant would be required to contribute to the Superannuation Account would be reduced by the amount required under the Canada Pension Plan.
That is all one sentence, and if anybody has the heart to go on to the second sentence I would be glad to show them the letter afterwards. The recipient did not understand anything about it, nor did I, and of course we had to ask for further clarification.
I am not a member of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to which I assume this bill will be referred, but I should hope that committee will approach it in the same fashion as another committee approached the election expenses bill, that is, in a non-partisan way. Many hon. members of that committee contributed a lot in the way of amendments to the bill, of which over 50 were accepted. In fact it was a learning experience for members of that committee.
Let me look specifically at Bill C-19. I think one of the most startling things to read is found on page 1 in the recommendation of His Excellency The Governor General which states that one of the aims of this bill is:
-to provide, in the manner prescribed for equality of status for males, and females under the Act-
I will have quite a bit to say about that, a little bit later.
On page 4, in Clause 7, we find reference to the election of a contributor in respect of self-employed earnings, and if you read further you see that there is reference to contributions of individuals who are members of a religious sect. They can elect not to make contributions, and this is on a once in a lifetime basis. I see no reference to a minimum age at which they will be allowed to excuse themselves, and I hope that the committee will see fit to change this by an amendment designating a specific minimum age because anyone who excuses himself under that election may decide years later he wants to come back in and will be forbidden to do so by the provisions of this bill as it now stands.

This is a very complex bill, so much so that I am sure the parliamentary secretary when he speaks later will want to clarify it.
On page 8 in Clause 10 we find reference to the amount of the maximum pensionable earnings. I can only say that I am very much in agreement with this, but I should like to speak about this matter as it relates to disability pensions referred to on page 12. In the proposed new Section 18 it does not clearly preclude an integrated act such as the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. If an individual is receiving a disability pension from the forces, and these two acts are integrated, I am curious to know whether the disability pension referred to in this bill is a service disability pension or a Canada Pension Plan disability pension. I think that should be clearly defined before this becomes the law of the land.
We note reference at page 25 to the effect that a surviving spouse under age 65 gets 37 V2 per cent plus, and over 65 gets 60 per cent of the pension contributed to on the death of his or her spouse. I suggest that anyone who thinks it only costs a husband of a household 40 per cent of his financial budget to run that household has no appreciation of what it costs. I think a housewife would need more than 60 per cent of her husband's pension in order to survive as a widow, and I suggest that 75 per cent would be a much more reasonable figure.
At page 33 there seems to be a clear contradiction in the explanatory notes in that part which reads:
The repeal of section 69 would remove the restriction in the amount of retirement pension that may be received by persons between 65 and 70 years of age while they are in receipt of employment earnings.
I suggest that one becomes confused when one reads at page 33, Clause 35, which starts out by saying "Sections 68 and 69 ... are repealed." Down at the bottom of the page we get figures and a statement to the effect that a person's pension will be reduced by 50 cents for each dollar which his employment earnings, for the months in the effective period in 1974 after the pension has become payable, but before the individual reaches 70 years of age, exceed that proportion of 12 times $95 that the number of months is of 12. I read this over several times, and eventually came to the conclusion that the government, when it talks in this bill about the effective period in 1974, is really referring to the ineffective period. That is the impression I got, that the effective period in 1974 is that period before this bill becomes an act and before the new amendment becomes law. Certainly that should be referred to as the ineffective period to clear up some of the obvious confusion.
Let me conclude these remarks by referring to page 22 again. I would express my unhappiness about the fact that this bill pretends that women are to get fair treatment under the Canada Pension Plan. The explanatory notes on the righthand page of this bill appear to have been written by a public relations officer rather than the minister, with his fine legal mind. We get a great buildup when we read these explanatory notes at page 22, particularly that statement which reads as follows:
This amendment would provide for equality of status for males and females under the Act.
That is rubbish and irony of the worst sort. The irony is, of course, that the bill provides for money to be paid to the man. How wrong can you be when you pretend to treat
April 17, 1974

females equally. You are giving them the big break in that you are paying money to a man who outlives them. That is ridiculous. I could quote from several press clippings to indicate that the press has been mislead about this clause of the bill. We find in the Toronto Star this heading, "Women to get same benefits as men". Then if we read Clause 25 we find this stated:
(d) a survivor's pension shall be paid to the surviving spouse, as determined pursuant to section 63-
If a woman dies, and if she was the head of the household at the time of death, the surviving spouse with dependent children will get some of the benefits that she has earned. Apparently that is the only concession made to women in this whole bill.
I would like to point out that in clause 25(2) (d) (ii) we have three paragraphs, (A), (B) and (C). This is totally confusing. It says that if the surviving spouse has reached 65 years of age:
(A)	had at the time of the death of the contributor reached 35 years of
age,
(B)	was at the time of the death of the contributor a surviving spouse
with dependent children, or
(C)	is disabled;
My question is does the "or" at the end of paragraph (B) mean that one must have (A) plus (B) on the one hand, or (C) on the other, or does one have the choice of (A), (B) or (C). Surely the minister's writers could have come up with something which would not lead to such confusion.
It confused the Toronto Star which in a headline states, "Women to get same benefits as men". Then the Montreal Star in an article said:
The second-
Referring to changes.
-designed to remove sex discrimination, will turn widows' pensions into survivors' pensions. That means that a husband whose wife has contributed to the plan at her job can collect benefits if she dies.
Mr. Speaker, what would give a fair deal to women would be if the housewife were allowed to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. This may have been what the minister hoped to receive credit for, while clearly avoiding giving this concession. I agree with the press release which came out today by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women which states, on page two, that they seek recognition of marriage as an economic unit as well as a social partnership. They recommend that during marriage 50 per cent of Canada Pension Plan contributions made by either husband or wife should be credited toward the pension buildup of the other spouse, whether or not the other spouse is in the paid labour market.
To me that would seem to represent justice. I believe this should be incorporated in legislation at the earliest possible time. This childishness of wondering whether to call a wife a house-spouse or house person, or contributor or survivor, possibly is a way to bring about discussion while the minister tries to get out of assuming responsibility. After slamming the minister for coming up with these words, if I may I should like to suggest that we could call the wife "counsel in the house" because counsel are well paid.
Canada Pension Plan
Believe me, wives are worth a lot more than this bill gives them. They have a right to be considered as full-fledged Canadian citizens. This legislation does not give that to them. The legislation does give them the knowledge that if they should die their husbands may be able to receive some monetary reward for having been married to them. I think this bill is an insult to womanhood.
With those words, Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude. I intend to vote for the bill. I hope the changes I have recommended will be accepted during the committee stage. I hope the minister gets this bill through fairly early and enjoys his day off.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate on a bill which is good and sound because, in essence, it endeavours to keep pace with changes in our society and the values held by Canadians. I was a little amused by the remarks made today at a certain point by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson), who seemed to claim fatherhood for the measures contained in this bill. I was amused, because we all remember what happened last summer in respect of the measure contained in this bill which would allow individual members of religious sects to be excluded from the provisions of the Canada Pension Plan in certain cases.
At that time another member of the same party took great exception to the measure. I refer to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). Until I receive notice to the contrary I assume that both the hon. member for Fraser Valley East and the hon. member for Crowfoot belong to the same party.
I find it difficult to understand how one member can claim fatherhood for the measures in this bill while another member of the same party was opposed to them at the time they came before us last. Be that as it may, the Canada Pension Plan came under unwarranted criticism last December by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
In a letter to the Toronto Star the Canadian Federation of Independent Business mounted an attack on the CPP stating, among other things, that in less than ten years there will be no money in the fund to provide benefits for all those Canadians working at that time. This is not so. The report that was tabled in this House by the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance in 1973 paints quite a different picture in respect of the Canada Pension Plan fund over the next decade. It indicates that if the present Canada Pension Plan contributions rates are maintained, the size of the Canada Pension Plan, far from disappearing as stated by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, will in fact increase from $6.6 billion to $20.3 billion by 1984.
Also the cost of the substantial Canada Pension Plan benefit improvements that were recently introduced by the government, and which came into effect on January 1 this year will be matched by increased revenues and contributions.
Finally, I find it worthwhile noting in connection with this fund, which is perhaps the envy of any other pension plan in the world for its help and substantial content, that approximately up to 70 per cent of Canada Pension Plan

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
benefits and administrative costs for the next decade are expected to be financed by the interest revenues accruing to the Canada Pension Plan fund. I have here figures that apply to the year 1974. The revenue from contributions is $1,074,000,000. The revenue from interest is $479 million, and the expenditures, the combined cost of benefits and administrative expenses, amounted to $437 million. This demonstrates the fact that revenue from interest at this point in time at least is greater than the cost of benefits and administrative expenses. I would say that represents pretty good management.
There are in this bill a number of very fine amendments which reflect a sense of fairness and social justice which the plan continually wishes to pursue. In addition to the examples that were given last night by the minister and other speakers, I should like to add a few which are worth putting on the record.
For instance the act provides now that when recipients of disability pensions reach age 65, payments of their disability pensions cease and they start receiving retirement pensions. It was originally intended that this change would occur the month after the beneficiary reached age 65, but through a quirk in the wording of the act the change is presently delayed by one month. One of the amendments proposed in this bill would remove this anomaly.
Similarly, there is a one month lag under existing law for the commencement of payment of widows or survivor's pension to a woman upon her reaching age 65. An amendment in the bill will correct this flaw. The same applies in the case of disability pension when that pension comes to a conclusion and the retirement pension takes over.
Another example is that the act now provides that wages earned by a contributor before his death, but paid after his death, cannot be taken into account for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan. An amendment is put forward to delete certain words in a section of the act which will remove this anomaly, taking effect as of January 1, 1975.
Another example is that the act now provides that the earnings of a self-employed person in the year of his death must be prorated whereas those of an employee are not. That means that if a self-employed contributor dies in the month of January, he could only be credited with one-twelfth of his actual earnings in January. The amendment removes this distinction and treats the self-employed person on the same basis as the employee contributor. This action will take place on January 1, 1975.
Another change deals with a contributor who holds two jobs simultaneously and who may expect to be assigned to two different year basic exemptions and may not have contributed on his total eligible earnings. The act allows such a person to elect to contribute on any such extra earnings. The amendments contained in the bill would clarify the wording of the section and extend the time limit for such election, and allow for an election by a representative of an incapacitated or deceased contributor.
It is a good step that the bill provides, in the case of a self-employed person who is not required to remit income tax by instalments, that he not be required to remit the

contribution to the Canada Pension Plan on an instalment basis.
There is another anomaly in the present act which prevents contributors from securing maximum disability pensions, although this is a minor loss in income. Nevertheless the contributor is required by the act to make contributions for a month in which he is not allowed to make a contribution. One of the amendments contained in the bill will remove this anomaly and pave the way for the payment of a maximum disability pension.
Another example, Mr. Speaker, relates to the fact that under the present legislation a survivor benefit which becomes payable in the month of January cannot be escalated in accordance with the cost of living index of the previous year. However, a survivor's benefit which becomes payable in December can be so escaled. In order to correct this anomalous situation in which the earlier pension is higher than the pension starting a month later, an amendment is proposed. It will apply the escalation factor to the pension payable in the month of January.
Another worth-while measure relates to a provision in the act that the required application for any Canada Pension Plan benefit can be made on behalf of an incapacitated contributor. In order to carry this principle to its ultimate conclusion, there are amendments in this bill that will allow appeals to be made on behalf of an incapacitated person at any three of the appeal levels.
Another example worth mentioning relates to the fact that at the present time the act allows for the denial of Canada Pension Plan benefits to persons who do not have a social insurance number. Among other things the bill proposes to remove this kind of penalty, and both ministers who are responsible for SINs will be authorized, along lines similar to those in the legislation governing old age security, to assign social insurance numbers to contributors and beneficiaries. We hope this particular amendment will be of some comfort, though perhaps limited, to the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) who has been struggling with a problem of one of his constituents regarding a social insurance number.
Like all those who have spoken before me, I support the changes contained in this bill and hope that there will be more to come in order to keep pace with the changing thinking in our society, with the changing expectations and attitudes toward work and retirement of Canadians.
Those who have spoken before me have already made the point about the desirability of changing the Canada Pension Plan in future so as to permit volunteer contributions by people who are not employed or self-employed but who do perform a valuable function in society without following a regular work pattern.
In the mail today we received a press release from the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. I should like to read a passage relating to the Canada Pension Plan which appears on page 2:
Recognition of marriage as an economic unit as well as a social partnership is a thrust of the proposal that during marriage 50 per cent of Canada Pension Plan contributions made by either husband or wife should be credited toward the pension build-up of the other spouse, whether or not the other spouse is in the paid labour market.
There is already an awareness in the country that makes it quite clear that a change of this nature would not only
April 17, 1974

be well received but would also reflect both a fact of life in our country and a desire that has been expressed in so many quarters.
Another change which will be most desirable in future is one affecting recipients of workmen's compensation benefits and pensions. These are paid usually to injured workmen or to women who, because of injury, must leave the labour force, sometimes for months or years. Consequently they cannot contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. It would be most desirable if we could treat workmen's Compensation payments as earnings, for purposes of contributing to the Canada Pension Plan. Such measure would be well received and would meet the aspirations and wishes of people, as expressed over the years.
May I suggest another measure which might be brought forward in future. It could be before this House in one year or so. It has to do with reducing the five-year period of contributions which is necessary before one can qualify for a disability pension. Some people who have been involved in accidents or who suffer from progressive diseases but who, nevertheless, have contributed for a few years, find that they have not contributed long enough to the Canada Pension Plan to qualify for a disability pension.
Instead of forcing them to turn to local or provincial welfare, under the Canada Assistance Plan it would be helpful if we could give them access to some form of disability pension, even if that pension is not as large as it would be for those who have met the five-year contribution criterion. At least they would receive the pension. This would help them. Definitely the fund is in such a healthy state that reducing the five-year contribution period to some lesser period would not affect seriously the level of moneys which have been built up in it over the years.
As I have said previously when answering criticisms, the fund is in an extremely healthy condition. If I understand actuarial studies correctly, it will be possible to support expenditures and administrative expenses with revenue from interest up until 1976. Between 1976 and 1984 revenue from interest alone will be high enough to subsidize 50 per cent, if not more, of expenses. So, the fund is in an extremely healthy condition.
Another desirable measure is suggested in the report issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare entitled, "Canada Pension Plan 1973". Page 9 deals in part with international agreements and reads:
On a wider scale, an exploratory three-day meeting was held in July, 1972 with officials of the United States Government to discuss problems related to the introduction of a general reciprocal agreement on social security. A similar meeting was held in September with United Kingdom officials for the same general purpose. In addition, the Government of Italy has expressed interest in negotiating a reciprocal agreement on social security. A meeting was held with Italian officials about a year ago and a further meeting is scheduled for the end of May to be attended by interested officials from both countries. In all three cases, National Revenue was involved from the point of view of coverage and contributions.
There is definitely great potential for international agreements with other countries which will permit the payment of Canada Pension Plan benefits to immigrants.
Canada Pension Plan
Such agreements will take into account total payments of various kinds made to various plans by the immigrant before arriving or settling in Canada. I urge the government to consider such measure. I am sure that such agreements will come about.
Looking to the future, I support the position taken last night eloquently by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He pleaded for a reduction in retirement age. We made great progress when we reduced the age of retirement from 70 to 65. Perhaps the time is ripe for us to give Canadians further options, that is, permit them to retire at an age of their choice. Of course their income from the Canada Pension Plan would be commensurate with their years of contribution and the age of retirement.
Instead of stressing the reduction of retirement age to age 60 it would make better sense, I suggest, if the government gave consideration to a system under which retirement might take place at any age. Of course, the earlier the retirement age, the smaller would be the payment. As I said, the fund is doing well, and will continue to do well for a number of years. It might do even better if we could determine the degree to which Canadians might wish to make larger contributions to the fund.
That brings me to my final point. Under the Canada Pension Plan there is an advisory committee. It is a good institution. It produces good ideas and gives the government an indication how the plan is functioning, what are its weaknesses, how it can be improved and what changes should be introduced from time to time. I see great merit in that institution.
I suggest that the government should consider seriously extending the system of consultation carried on through such advisory committees. It should do this on a broader basis, and consult Canadians regularly. For instance, the government could determine what Canadians think of the plan and how much they would be willing to pay into the fund, to achieve those very things which have been proposed in this debate, among which is earlier retirement.
Methods similar to those used at present could be used. For instance, when people get their monthly Old Age Security or Family Allowance cheques, they often find in the envelope excellent printed material which deals with nutrition or other messages the government wishes to communicate. By similar means the people could be asked at regular intervals what they think the Canada Pension Plan should offer in addition to what it is offering, and how much more they are willing to pay to achieve certain goals. Questionnaires might be sent to recipients of Old Age Security and Family Allowances.
I appreciate that the sample obtained would be very small and far from perfect. Nevertheless, it would be a way of assessing those in receipt of a substantial social security measure as to their views about the Canada Pension Plan, to consult them, and put to them the cost of improvements, as well as asking whether they would support the idea of greater contributions than are made at present. By so doing the government and politicians would be in a better position to guage the will of Canadians as to what the future of the Canada Pension Plan ought to be.

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
We could determine whether there is the support we seem to sense, but for which we do not have any tangible proof, with regard to retirement earlier than age 65. It would also determine whether there is a willingness on the part of Canadians to make more substantial contributions to the fund which would in turn permit the fund to pay more substantial pensions and make them available at an earlier age.
The Canada Pension Plan is a very fascinating scheme of social security which reinforces the democratic structure of this country. It certainly reinforces the federal-provincial fibre of this nation. As members know, excess moneys in the fund are invested in provincial securities with a term of maturity of 20 years.
Since the inception of the Canada Pension Plan I understand that substantial funds have been invested in this way. In 1972-73 these excess moneys amounted to $971 million, which were invested in securities of the provinces and Crown agencies. From the inception of the plan up until March 31 of last year the total investment amounted to no less than $5 Vi billion, no small sum. It is definitely a source of capital that comes in very handy for the provinces for their own public works and other measures that serve the needs of Canadians in each province of this country.
Apart from the aspect of strengthening the fibre of confederation, there is a potential element in the Canada Pension Plan which is promising and exciting. If we could look beyond the scope of the advisory committee and consult Canadians from coast to coast as to their willingness to continue to respond at the present or lower levels, or hopefully at higher levels in order to make available retirement or disability pensions at a greater rate than at present, that would reflect their willingness and readiness to make these contributions available. By doing it in that way we could truly put into effect a fine concept of democracy, something which I suppose was in the minds of those who originally designed this very fine plan.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-19 to amend the Canada Pension Plan. During the debate on Bill C-224 we indicated our support for that particular amendment. On this occasion we have also indicated our support for some restriction of the debate so that this bill can have quick passage.
During the last debate we encouraged the minister to take action in many areas where we felt there was discrimination and hardships. At that time I made a personal appeal to the minister to outline in more detail his philosophy regarding the Canada Pension Plan and, in particular, its relationship to the orange paper on social security.
It is true the minister has acted on many of the recommendations we suggested in the last session, but I find it particularly disturbing that he has not responded to the more important and fundamental issue of providing the details that I believe must be available to ensure the intelligent public debate that he purports to be necessary for developing a total security strategy.

Following the federal-provincial conference on February 19 and 20 of this year there were numerous communiques and press releases which indicated a consensus on many of the issues we proposed in the past, including the very important issue of equality. However, it was readily apparent from the releases that the federal government had not addressed itself to the principle of equal rights for women.
They also announced that this major issue relating to women, particularly in those areas of family farms or small businesses, or indeed at home as housewives, should be studied further and referred to the Canada Pension Plan advisory committee and to the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. I would refer to this as a typical example of the shuffle-the-problem type of game.
Earlier this year June Menzies, the vice-chairman of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, presented a discussion paper entitled The Canada Pension Plan and Women. Actually it was presented in January of this year. Surely we are not to believe that the Canada Pension Plan advisory committee has been sitting by idly ignoring these issues and not reporting directly to the minister.
The problem that bothers me most, and I feel it is a real insult to the intelligence of this House, is that in his opening remarks yesterday the minister made reference to the discussion paper on housewives and the Canada Pension Plan, which was presented to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on April 4. I plan to make some detailed reference to that later.
To summarize, the government and the minister presented to this House the orange paper on social security, of which the Canada Pension Plan is a very vital component. We are presented with ad hoc amendments v/hich I admit add substantially to the existing legislation. However, we have not had access to detailed information from the department, and we have not had the positive statements required of the minister in the proper forum to discuss in detail the total social security program, particularly as it relates to the Canada Pension Plan. Rather, we have been confronted by a smokescreen, first in the presentation of an inadequately detailed orange paper and now with an ill-prepared paper discussing housewives and the Canada Pension Plan. As I already indicated I will be making some comments about that particular discussion paper a little later.
At the outset I referred to several matters which my party supported in the past and which are now included in this bill. They correct some of the vast injustices of the program. As has been done by other members, I wish to congratulate the minister for bringing in these changes. The main purpose of this bill is to ensure that benefits are paid to survivors of female contributors on an equal basis with survivors of male contributors. We have long recognized this discriminatory feature against female contributors, and have repeatedly requested these changes over the last few years. It is also important to note the provinces have requested similar changes in the past, notably at the most recent federal-provincial conference. In effect the amounts of the benefits paid on application will depend on the same age, health and dependent children qualifications as now apply to widows.
April 17, 1974

The repeal of the disincentive to work between ages of 65 and 70 has long been recommended by many organizations, including the Advisory Committee of the Canada Pension Plan.
The statistics related to low income indicate that when the head of the household is between the ages of 65 to 69, the incidence of low income is 26.7 per cent; when he is 70 years of age or older, 29.1 per cent. The low income incidence among unattached individuals in the same age categories is of 50 per cent and 65.5 per cent.
With such a high incidence of low incomes among the aged, and with the difficulties our senior citizens have experienced in living with rampant inflation and a spiralling cost of living, I find it difficult to comprehend why this disincentive was originally introduced into the plan.
The completion of adjusting the years maximum pensionable earnings is an additional feature of the bill, along with a new formula for determining the year's basic exemption. Again these proposals are in keeping with the recommendations of the federal-provincial conference. I must add, however, that this is a further example of inadequate information being disseminated to the public. I have been contacted by several small businesses and labour groups who do not comprehend the impact these proposed changes will have on their businesses, many of them marginal in operation, or on the take home pay of those working in such businesses. Surely the minister can supply such data so that the individuals concerned may fully understand the impact of the changes.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) made reference to Bill C-190 when he spoke a few moments ago. May I simply say I was personally pleased to see the amendments proposed in Bill C-190 during the last session included in the present bill. The presentation made by the Old Order of Amish and Mennonites to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Services was for me a moving experience. Their belief that their own religious community, not the government or any outside insurance plan, should carry the responsibilities for the welfare and support of its members is a refreshing testimony to the community spirit. Their contribution to the surrounding community, their fellow man, and to the international community is an example all Canadians could seek to emulate.
Several technical changes have been introduced. They include provisions to improve the appeal system, provisions for self-employed to remit CPP contributions on an instalment basis, changes more in keeping with present divorce laws, provision for payment of disabled contributors, child benefits for natural or legally adopted children acquired by pensioners after the onset of disability, provision for the write-off of certain debts, relaxation of the four year limit on employee corrections to records of earnings, and the repeal of the prohibition which prevents persons who do not have a social insurance number from receiving CPP benefits.
A major problem which has not been adequately covered is one related to the delay in processing applications made not only on retirement but in particular by those applying for permanent disability pensions. In addition, since the
Canada Pension Plan
program is convenient for many employees, consideration should be given to allowing them to invest money towards their retirement above the present legal limits, if they so desire.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the fundamental issue I raised in the House on October 30, 1973, and referred to in my opening comments today. What role does the CPP play in the entire social security strategy? The Annual Report on Health and Welfare for 1972-73, referring to the Canada Pension Plan implies we are dealing with a social insurance plan:
The Canada Pension Plan was established by act of Parliament which received Royal Assent on April 3, 1965, and was proclaimed in force on May 5 of the same year. The plan is designed to be entirely self-supporting; all benefits and administrative costs are financed from contributions of employees, employers and self-employed persons, together with the interest earned from the investment of funds.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt the impression conveyed to the Canadian public is that this is a social insurance program. It must be re-emphasized that the Canada Pension Plan was introduced as a contributory social insurance program for members of the Canadian labour force, with three basic objectives:
1.	To guarantee an income-related pension to every member of the labour force.
2.	To provide basic social insurance to each labour force member and dependents in the event of death or total disability.
3.	To provide a source of capital to the provinces.
We have established a program which is complex and poorly understood by the Canadian people. The government and the minister have convinced the majority of Canadians that the Canada Pension Plan is a pure social insurance program when in reality it contains many non-earnings-related benefits, giving it many features consistent with a welfare program.
We have a government which talks of a social security strategy, which makes ad hoc amendments to existing legislation, which distracts us with working papers, but which refuses to define the role of the CPP within the context of an over-all income security policy.
Let me give an illustration from my speech last year. When the guaranteed income supplement payments began in 1967, the year in which the Canada Pension Plan commenced, the Guaranteed Income Supplement was initially intended as a temporary program to be phased out when the CPP matured in 1967.
In the 1970 white paper on income security the government proposed to establish the guaranteed income supplement as a permanent program, to continue universal old age security payments, and to amend the Canada Pension Plan. The proposed CPP amendments were to eliminate two problems as defined by the white paper: first, gaps remaining in the income security system, particularly for widows and disabled people; secondly, CPP contributions and benefits had not kept pace with the growth in average Canadian wages. The suggested changes in the CPP amendments were to increase substantially widows and disability benefits, and to increase retirement benefits
1522

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
through selective increases in the earnings ceilings. These changes obviously emphasized the welfare aspects of the plan.
By design we have a government that discusses the development of a social insurance strategy in which the CPP has received top priority. The government has given the impression that this is a form of pure social insurance and refuses to define, or what is more likely cannot define, the role of the Canada Pension Plan in our fragmented social security system. In effect we have a plan which has features of social insurance, therefore not requiring internal subsidies. In addition, we have a plan which has welfare features, including subsidies paid by the taxpayers, similar to other income support programs. And, what is most tragic, these subsidies in many instances are paid to those with the least need rather than to that large segment living in or near poverty.
At the outset I indicated that I wanted to spend some time discussing what I feel to be a most important document, and that is the discussion paper on housewives and the Canada Pension Plan which was introduced to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on April 4, 1974. I have some comments I wish to make about this, but to comment properly, Mr. Speaker, and with complete understanding, I should like to quote from the discussion paper and then make some observations following that.
The introduction to this paper on housewives and the Canada Pension Plan is as follows:
This is a time of reappraisal concerning the position of women in society and in the home. Certain traditional assumptions and values are being questioned and changed. This relates both to the increasing participation of women in the economic work force of the nation, and to changing attitudes concerning the position of women within the fundamental unit of Canadian society-the family.
This basic reappraisal bears upon the Canada Pension Plan in two main respects: (1) certain provisions within the plan accord different treatment to male and female contributors and beneficiaries, and this has been questioned; (2) views have been expressed that housewives who remain at home, and do not draw salaries as members of the working force, should be enabled to participate in the Canada Pension Plan.
Action is now underway with respect to the first issue. The government of Canada, with the full agreement of all provincial governments, is placing legislation before the 1974 session of parliament to establish full equality of treatment for male and female contributors and beneficiaries.
The second issue was discussed by the federal and provincial welfare ministers at a meeting in Edmonton in February, 1974, as a part of their review of the social security system. All governments recognized that there were complex difficulties associated with the implementation of this objective. The ministers agreed, however, that the various possible approaches to meeting this objective should be given serious study. The issues involved need to be examined not only by governments, but by the public at large. This paper has been prepared, therefore, in the hope that it will provoke wider public discussion of the issues, and that from this discussion the best answers may emerge.
It should be noted that while this paper speaks of the "housewife", since it is most frequently the woman who remains at home to look after the interests of the family unit, the same principles, of course, apply also in cases when men remain at home for this purpose. However, the term "housewife" was used in preference to the more general but less appealing term "housespouse".
This is the issue as defined in this paper:
The central features of the issue, the considerations involved, and the practical range of options for the future were set forth clearly by

the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. In the words of the Commission:
"With rare exceptions, the woman who stays at home depends on her husband for money. While she may receive a family allowance cheque, the money is spent on the cost of keeping a child and cannot be regarded as payment for its care. Unfortunately we have no over-all solution for the financial dependency of housewives. But there is one area in which steps could be taken to give them some financial independence at least in their later years. Housewives should be entitled to pensions in their own right under the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan.
"The housewife who remains at home is just as much a producer of goods and services as the paid worker, and in our view she should also have the opportunity to provide for a more financially secure future. Canada has given some of its workers an opportunity to do this through the Canada and the Quebec Pension Plans. To neglect to do the same for some three and one-half million other workers in the home is to ignore the essential nature of their work.
"The Canada and the Quebec Pension Plans do not entirely ignore housewives since they provide for a pension for a widow of a contributor. In other words, these plans recognize that a widow should benefit from her husband's contributions.
"This is in keeping with the concept of marriage as a partnership. But in recognizing only the rights of a widow to a pension on the basis of her husband's contributions, the plans go only part way. For example, in the case of a marriage breakdown, the former wife loses all claim to a widow's pension. This can cause hardship when the breakdown occurs late in life and the wife has had insufficient time to build up a reasonable pension through her own paid work. A second wife may reap the benefits of the contributions made by the husband during his first marriage.
"Even if a divorced or separated woman enters paid employment, the pension she earns may be adversely affected by the years she spent in the home as a housewife. Pensions are related to earnings and her earnings prior to, during and after marriage are averaged over the number of years she could have been employed, and this includes the time that she remained in the home. While some provision is made for reducing the number of years to be averaged, there will be cases in which a divorced or separated woman will be unable to work a sufficient number of years to make up for a non-earning period as a housewife.
"For all of these reasons provision must be made for the participation of housewives in the Canada or the Quebec Pension Plan. A comprehensive study will be required to determine the best way of achieving this... However, two approaches seem to us to have considerable merit...
"(i) crediting to the spouse remaining at home a portion of the contributions of the employed spouse and those contributions made by the employer on the employed spouse's behalf, and (ii) on an optional basis, permitting the spouse at home to contribute as a self-employed worker."
This document in many ways, I feel, is a perfect camouflage of the government's inability to ensure women's full participation as contributors to, and recipients of benefits from, the CPP. As I indicated earlier, as with the orange paper we have been presented with little information to promote intelligent debate.
Under the present plan, which I indicated earlier was subsidized by the government in many instances, will the minister be prepared to subsidize a rich 64 year old housewife who can contribute to the Canada Pension Plan rather than utilize that subsidy to assist the poor 64 year old housewife who cannot contribute to the Canada Pension Plan? Would he subsidize a 64 year old housewife under the CPP and ignore one who is 84 years of age?
There is no intelligent way of discussing this document or this paper without presenting dollar amounts involved
April 17, 1974

per person. When we are being asked to make a choice, on a personal basis or otherwise, in respect of any financial matter or, in this instance, when government spending is involved, we must ask for two important sets of figures: first the dollars you will pay and, secondly, the dollars you will get back. Let me turn as an example to the bottom of page 4, and I should like to quote from this page which deals with mandatory alternatives. It states:
This approach would certainly give recognition to work in the home as regular employment, and would provide a measure of financial independence to the housewife. However, it seems unlikely that most Canadians would find this to be a satisfactory alternative. It is necessary to ask how many Canadian families would consider it acceptable for the government to intervene in this way in the financial arrangements made between husband and wife? Also, how many families would consider it acceptable to be required to make additional Pension Plan contributions from the same level of family income?
I would simply suggest in respect of such a question that Canadians cannot make an honest appraisal, in order to give an honest answer to that kind of question, without a knowledge as to the dollars in and dollars out to which I referred previously.
The crux of the issue in this document relates to the second point on page 2. I quoted this before but I want to come back to it. It states:
"(ii) on an optional basis, permitting the spouse at home to contribute as a self-employed worker."
The housewife very frequently wants to be included under the Canada Pension Plan at the same contribution rates and with the same benefit rate as any other Canadian, whether it be her husband, a career woman or someone else. I suggest that this working paper makes no attempt to address itself to this problem but simply waffles by summarizing five points at page 10, proposing these as an , answer to the problem in respect of equal rights as between men and women. Let me quote this, Mr. Speaker: The most important considerations, however, are issues involving basic social equity, and the future operation of the Canada Pension Plan, and private insurance and pension plans. These issues may be summarized as follows:
1.	If housewives are allowed to participate in the Canada Pension Plan on a voluntary basis, this option would tend to favour wives in families having the willingness and financial ability to participate. Wives in lower income families would have an extremely limited capacity to take advantage of such an opportunity.
2.	Can the needs of wives at home be considered separate and apart from those of other individuals who undergo long periods of no earnings because of unemployment, ill health, extended education, and other reasons?
3.	If housewives with earnings are permitted to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan on a voluntary basis, should any provision for voluntary participation be extended to housewives with part-time earnings, and other part-time and low income workers?
4.	If an opportunity were extended to some or all wage earners to supplement their Canada Pension Plan coverage on a voluntary basis, a situation would be created whereby wage earners could transfer their coverage under private pension plans to the Canada Pension Plan. The differences in funding arrangements between the Canada Pension Plan and private plans would provide a substantial incentive for many to make such transfers. If this were done on a large scale, it could seriously undermine the position of private pension plans.
5.	Actuarial reports which the government has tabled in Parliament from time to time indicate that the financial provisions of the Canada Pension Plan will have to be reviewed at some future date. If such a future review should lead to an increase in contribution rates, would volunteer participants be allowed to reduce or withdraw their
Canada Pension Plan
participation? If this were permitted, the increased costs of the pensions credits, accumulated by the volunteer participants would be passed on to the participants who are required to contribute to the Plan on a compulsory basis. The equity of such an arrangement could be the subject of serious criticism if the bulk of volunteer participants came from higher income families, and if large numbers of compulsory participants were comprised of low wage earners. These consequences could be avoided if volunteer participants, once allowed to participate, were required to maintain their participation; or, if allowed to reduce or withdraw their participation, were required to accept a reduction in the value of their accumulated pension credits. Such alternatives, however, would likely be considered as acts of bad faith on the part of the government.
As I suggested previously, if the minister is truly interested in resolving this critical issue of equal rights for men and women involved with the Canada Pension Plan, he could help by presenting simple dollar examples and illustrations for various individuals or people involved.
Referring again to page 8 of this paper let me quote from paragraph (b) which states:
The family could be allowed to assign a dollar value to work in the home (perhaps within some prescribed limits), which would be over and above to wages earned by the husband, and contributions could be made in the name of the housewife based on this amount. This would permit the housewife to build up her own pension credits without any decrease in the family unit's basic protection. However, it would also mean that the family would have to pay additional contributions to the Plan out of the same level of income.
I should like to emphasize again that this is another example of why the Canadian family could not make a valued judgment of such a statement without a dollar presentation, or a proper analysis in respect of a particular family. I strongly urge the minister to present such figures to the House, or to the standing committee, so that an appropriate analysis can be made.
I am deeply concerned about a basic point that has not been discussed in this particular working paper to which I have been referring. If we consider the pensions payable to retired married couples and those payable to a retired person living alone, whether he be single, divorced, a widow or a widower, using as an example old age security, we find that a couple will get exactly twice the amount a single person receives; and if we look at the guaranteed income supplement we find that a couple receives almost twice the amount a single person receives. The minister stated to the House and to the standing committee that the general pattern around the world in respect of government pensions would indicate that a couple receives almost twice the pension received by a single person. That being so, surely a couple should receive under the Canada Pension Plan an amount exactly double that received by a single person?
If this logic is good, then surely splitting the Canada Pension Plan credits, as one of the alternatives suggested, would be at odds with the existing plan and would be of no value? Therefore, only by bringing in housewives with the same contribution rates and the same benefit rates as workers will we achieve this particular end.
The hon. member from British Columbia who spoke earlier referred to the policy paper on women presented to our national convention, and I agree with the two statements he made. If the minister is sincere in implementing this important principle of equality as between men and women by removing the injustices and discrimination against women, surely he will present a detailed dollar
