analysis of the various proposals, illustrating individual examples.
Only in this way can we have a proper analysis and appropriate decisions with regard to the plan and regain the confidence of the people of Canada. If the minister in searching for a solution, and wishing to gain the support of the House in these areas I have talked about, would present this particular material to the standing committee, or to the House, and consider the facts I have raised, I think this would go a long way toward improving the program and giving equal rights to men and women across Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak during this debate on the second reading of Bill C-19 to amend the Canada Pension Plan. This is the second major bill to amend the Canada Pension Plan that the government has introduced since it began, a year ago, a review with the provinces of Canada's social security system. The first bill was passed by Parliament last session.
The bill we are debating will fulfil the commitment respecting the first round of agreements with regard to the Canada Pension Plan reached with the provinces in October last year, and will give effect to the second round of agreements that were concluded with the provinces just two months ago in Edmonton. It is important to summarize the main features of the bill. It proposes full equality of treatment for male and female contributors and beneficiaries under the Canada Pension Plan.
It proposes repeal of the earnings and retirement tests under this plan so that contributors aged 65 and over can draw all Canada Pension Plan retirement benefits they have earned without regard to subsequent earnings. It proposes a new formula for determining the year's maximum pensionable earnings, which is the earnings ceiling for the plan, so that future benefits and revenue will reflect the advances in the Canadian wage level that have been occurring during the last decade.
The new formula also provides that once the base for calculating new benefits and determining fund revenues is brought up to date it will keep pace with further increases in the average earnings of Canadian industrial workers. Bill C-19 proposes modification in the current formula for determining the basic exemption for the plan so that Canadians at low income levels will have a greater opportunity to participate more fully in the Canada Pension Plan.
The bill re-introduces the provisions that were placed before Parliament last session in Bill C-190 regarding the exemption of persons from the plan on grounds of religious conviction. I notice the hon. member who spoke so long on that particular aspect just appeared and now appears to be disappearing. Then there is the liberalization of the provisions dealing with payment of legal expenses, the measures concerning financial administration of the plan, as well as the negotiation of international agreements. These proposals enjoyed wide support in Parliament but could not be enacted before the end of the last session.

This bill contains a large number of technical amendments that rectify minor errors, inequities and anomalies the department has uncovered in the administration of the plan. Generally speaking these technical proposals do not affect a large number of contributors and beneficiaries but are important to those directly affected. In almost all instances they operate to their advantage.
The review of the Canada Pension Plan has not been completed. Priority subjects are still outstanding. These include the coverage of housewives, early retirement provisions under the plan, the structure and level of the Canada Pension Plan disability and survivor benefits, and the degree to which the needs of the disabled, orphans, widows and widowers should be met by a social insurance program such as the Canada Pension Plan, and the extent to which these needs should be met by income supplementation programs.
Everyone recognizes there are very complex problems raised by the various proposals that have been received concerning the participation of housewives. It is felt that it would be unwise to come to a hasty conclusion before these problems can be thoroughly studied. Various possibilities, such as voluntary contribution and the splitting of pension credits, should be carefully examined during the ensuing years.
It is also desirable to have substantial public discussion of the issues involved. This matter has been referred to the Canada Pension Plan advisory committee and to the advisory Council on the Status of Women for their consideration. In order to have a discussion of the issue within Parliament, the minister has tabled before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs a paper entitled "Housewives and the Canada Pension Plan". These initiatives of the minister should provoke public discussion of the issue both inside and outside Parliament. This will assist in determining what are the best answers.
At the same time work will continue on the other studies mentioned, and it is expected that this will be finished within the target period for completing the review of Canada's social security system. The result of these and other studies cannot of course be predicted, but it may well be they will call for the introduction of a further bill to amend the Canada Pension Plan.
Let us examine more closely the major provisions of Bill C-19. The most noteworthy changes proposed by the bill in terms of principle are the provisions for the equal treatment of male and female contributors and beneficiaries. We can take pleasure in seeing them in the bill. The equal treatment of Canadian men and women is a principle to which this government is firmly committed, and is being reflected in further legislation to be considered during the current session of Parliament. The discussion paper recently tabled in the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs states:
This is a time of reappraisal concerning the position of women in society and in the home. Certain traditional assumptions and values are being questioned and changed. This relates both to the increasing participation of women in the economic work force of the nation, and to changing attitudes concerning the position of women within the fundamental unit of Canadian society-the family.
It is most interesting in this regard to introduce here the thoughts of my own wife, that there comes a time in the
April 17, 1974

family unit when a man is so occupied, as we are here in Ottawa, that the woman realizes there is a part she can usefully play in life, and that she should look for a means by which she can be an equal contributor to the productivity of the nation.
Bill C-19 provides striking and tangible evidence of the rate and degree to which traditional assumptions and attitudes on the role of women in Canadian society have changed. The end of the traditional phase of the Canada Pension Plan lies about two years in the future, yet before the plan is fully mature we are already concluding that we should remove the basic distinctions between males and females which were built into the plan with a broad measure of public support a few short years ago.
Distinctions to be abolished by Bill C-19 include the provision in the Canada Pension Plan that upon the death of the male contributor the surviving widow is automatically eligible for a pension equal to 60 per cent of her husband's actual or imputed retirement pension if she is 65 or older. If the surviving widow is between 45 and 65 years of age, or below age 45 and is disabled or has dependent children, she is eligible for a pension equal to 37 V2 per cent of her husband's actual or imputed retirement pension, plus a flat rate component which now amounts to some $33.76 a month. Lesser amounts are paid to widows between 35 and 45 years of age, and not disabled, or who do not have dependent children.
In addition, when a male contributor dies or becomes disabled, his children automatically become eligible for a benefit that at present amounts to $33.76 per month for each child, or some variation for families with more than four children. On the other hand, when a female contributor dies or becomes disabled, her surviving widower is eligible for a widower's pension only when he is disabled and dependent upon his wife, and the children become eligible for benefit only if they were wholly or substantially maintained by their mother. These differences, it should be noted, have existed notwithstanding the fact that the contribution rate to the plan is the same for male and female contributors.
Bill C-19 proposes the complete removal of these distinctions. The effect of this change, if and when enacted, will be that surviving spouses and children of deceased or disabled female contributors will, in future, qualify for the same benefits, and under the same conditions as those that now apply in respect of the surviving spouses and children of male contributors. The current provision which limits the payment of one benefit for each child will be maintained, and it will be paid upon the death or disability of the first spouse.
An important clause in the bill proposes retroactive eligibility, but not retroactive payment, for the surviving spouses and children of female contributors who died or became disabled prior to proclamation of this bill. In other words, the bill proposes that after proclamation widowers and the children of female contributors who died, or became disabled prior to proclamation, will from that point in time become eligible to receive benefits as though the Canada Pension Plan had always accorded equal treatment to male and female contributors and beneficiaries.
Canada Pension Plan
This particular proposal of the bill will, it is estimated, benefit about 30,000 individuals.
Those who may be affected by this retroactive feature should note that benefits under the Canada Pension Plan are only payable upon application. Potential beneficiaries of female contributors who died or became disabled prior to proclamation of the bill should consult a CPP district office about their eligibility for a benefit as soon as possible after the bill comes into force.
Another important group of provisions in Bill C-19 deal with the repeal of the earnings and retirement tests. The Canada Pension Plan at present provides that retirement pensions can only be paid to contributors between the ages of 65 and 70 if they have retired from regular employment. Furthermore, if a pensioner, after retirement and under the age of 70, draws wages in excess of $95 a month, the act now requires that his CPP pension be reduced by 50 per cent of his wages between $95 and $155 a month, and by the full amount of his employment earnings in excess of $155 a month.
Bill C-19 proposes the removal of all these restrictions, and so, if and when the bill becomes law, all contributors who are 65 years of age or older will be able to draw all of the retirement pension they have earned whether or not they continue to work and receive wages. It is estimated that these changes will provide an immediate increase for about 5,000 current CPP retirement pensioners, and will result in the payment of perhaps 30,000 additional retirement pensions in 1975.
The removal of the earnings and retirement tests from the Canada Pension Plan could prove to be one of the more costly reforms. It could, over the next 10 to 15 years, turn out to be more costly even than providing full escalation of CPP benefits in accordance with increases in the cost of living. Much will depend upon the number of contributors who will decide to work beyond age 65 and to apply for CPP retirement pensions when they reach age 65.
Virtually half of the contributors who applied for CPP retirement pensions during 1973 were 66 years of age or older, and the proportion of applicants who were 67 years or older was slightly in excess of 30 per cent of all applicants for 1973 CPP retirement pensions. This is interesting in the face of the frequently expressed assumption that most Canadians will shortly be wanting to retire by age 60 or even less. The experience with the Canada Pension Plan indicates that notwithstanding the criticisms of some that retirement at age 65 is an outdated concept, we are still a considerable distance from having universal observance of the age 65 retirement practice. Consequently if contributors who hitherto have been delaying their applications for CPP retirement pensions now decide, in overwhelming proportions, to apply for retirement pensions as soon as they reach age 65, it could have a substantial financial impact on the plan.
Of course persons between 65 and 70 still have the option of not taking their retirement pension, but continuing to contribute to the fund to build up their eventual benefit. A proportion of contributors may conclude that it is in their interest to do this.

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to turn to the provisions of the bill that deal with the YMPE, or earnings ceiling of the plan. The earnings ceiling, as members are aware, plays a critical role in shaping the revenue and benefit structure of the Canada Pension Plan.
At the October meeting of federal-provincial welfare ministers it was agreed that the CPP earnings ceiling should be brought into line with the one applying to the Quebec Pension Plan, and should then be increased by 12 V2 per cent a year until it caught up to the average earnings of Canadian industrial workers and, once this was achieved, the ceiling should be kept in line with the earnings of the average Canadian industrial workers. The first steps toward carrying out this agreement were taken when parliament, last session, passed the bill to establish the plan's YMPE at $6,000 for 1974 and at $7,400 for 1975. Bill C-19 contains the proposals for carrying out the other elements of this agreement.
Bill C-19, and the bill passed in the last session, go a long way toward establishing fair and equitable treatment for the nation's retired, disabled, widows, widowers and orphans.
Maximum initial retirement pensions under the plan now stand at $101.41 a month. If the bill is passed, initial maximum CPP retirement pensions should reach a level of about $250 a month by 1980, and $350 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of close to 250 per cent in about ten years' time.
Maximum CPP disability pensions now stand at $125.95 a month. Passage of the bill should raise these pensions to about $225 a month by 1980, and $315 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of close to 170 per cent in ten years' time.
Maximum CPP widow and widower pensions for beneficiaries under the age of 65 now stand at $79.86 a month. Passage of the bill should raise these pensions to about $135 a month by 1980, and $185 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of over 130 per cent in ten years' time.
Maximum CPP widow and widower pensions for beneficiaries 65 years of age and older now stand at $73.75 a month. Passage of the bill should raise these pensions to about $145 a month by 1980, and to $210 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of over 180 per cent in the next ten years.
Basic orphans and disabled contributor child benefits now stand at $33.76 a month. These should rise to about $45 a month by 1980 and $55 a month by 1985.
The increase in child benefits is not provided by this bill, but was accomplished by the bill that Parliament passed last session. This bill does, however, propose that in future they should also be paid in respect of the children of female contributors who die or become disabled. All of these increased benefit rates would be fully escalated thereafter according to increases in the cost of living. It should also be noted that in 1985 we are likely to have three times the 500,000 CPP beneficiaries that we now have.

The updating of the earnings formula that is now in the plan provides that all contributor earnings are updated according to movements in the YMPE; so, sharp increases in the YMPE produce a sharp updating of past earnings at all levels.
These increases in CPP benefits are quite substantial. Still, they do not tell the full story of achievement that has been realized in our social security reforms. During the last year other parts of our social security system have been modernized and, when these improvements are combined with Bill C-19, they produce results of almost dramatic proportions.
For example the income situation of a couple at retirement in a single wage earner family should be considered. A little over a year ago the maximum CPP/OAS income of this couple was about $245 a month; today it is $320 a month. In 1980 it may be in excess of $525 a month; and in 1985 it should be in the order of $700 a month. Seven hundred dollars a month is reasonably close to the average wage of today's industrial worker.
Members might reflect upon the situation of the widow under 65 years of age, with four children under the age of 18. A little over a year ago her CPP survivor benefit and family allowance payments would have amounted to about $200 a month; today they are about $295 a month. In 1980 they should be over $400 a month; and in 1985 they could be in the order of $550 a month. The government is justified in taking considerable pride in this record of achievements.
The Canada Pension Plan has an earnings exemption, called the year's basic exemption, which sets the minimum annual earnings an individual must have in order to contribute to the plan. This exemption is now set at 12 per cent of the earnings ceiling. The possibility therefore arises that if the earnings ceiling is increased quickly, substantial numbers of contributors at the bottom end of the income scale could lose the continuity of their CPP coverage, and so lose some of the advantages of this bill. To prevent this from happening the bill proposes that the basic exemption formula be altered from 12 to 10 per cent of the earnings ceiling. This change, therefore, will provide greater opportunities for people at the lower income levels to participate more fully in the Canada Pension Plan.
The bill also proposes deletion of a special provision that has applied to self-employed persons, namely, the requirement that they must earn at least one and one third of the year's basic exemption to qualify as contributors under the plan. It is proposed that this distinction be removed so that employees and self-employed persons will be on the same footing for exemption purposes. This measure should assist a number of self-employed Canadians in seasonal activities like farming and fishing, where fluctuating conditions sometimes reduce incomes to marginal levels, in maintaining the continuity of their CPP coverage.
There are numerous proposals in the bill which can be labelled as miscellaneous, technical and administrative amendments. The minister has taken the opportunity presented by the bill to carry out some house cleaning in what is a very complex act. These proposals, which for the most part rectify inequities, anomalies, errors, and
April 17, 1974

ambiguities that have been uncovered over a period of time, should be incorporated as a tidying up procedure.
I should like to draw the House's attention to the fact that CPP benefit payments, and the costs associated with administering the plan, are not paid from tax revenues, but come out of the earnings of the Canada Pension Plan investment fund and contributions. Bill C-19 proposes no change in this aspect of the plan. There is every likelihood that the new CPP benefit levels will, in the coming years, obviate the need for some payments to be made from the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Canada Assistance Plan, and a wide range of other programs that are financed out of general tax revenues. Bill C-19 proposes no change in existing CPP contribution rates.
Some of the costs of the new benefit levels will come out of the substantial amounts of additional contribution revenues that will be generated by the new earnings ceilings for 1974 and 1975 that were established last year and by the new earnings ceiling formula that is contained in this bill. This revenue source will probably produce additional contribution revenues of over $100 million in 1974, $200 million in 1975, $300 million in 1977, and higher amounts, naturally, in subsequent years. The rest will come from the revenue producing features that are now in the plan.
Since the operation of the Canada Pension Plan began, all benefit payments and administrative expenses of the plan have been paid out of interest earned by the Canada Pension Plan investment fund. Contributions, in effect, have all been invested in the purchase of substantial amounts of provincial securities.
This situation should continue to prevail throughout 1974, as it is estimated that interest credited to the plan during 1974 will be in the range of $475 to $500 million, while benefit payments and administrative expenses will amount to around $470 million.
The amendments that were made to the plan last year, and the ones now being proposed, therefore have substantial implications for the financial structure of the plan toward the end of the century. Consequently the revenue-producing features of the plan will have to be reviewed much sooner than would otherwise be the case.
If the bill is passed it is anticipated that the balance in the Canada Pension Plan account will continue to grow over the next 15 years. This time frame could, of course, change if additional amendments to the plan are made at the end of the social security review. In any event, there should be ample time to carry out an orderly review of the plan's financial structure and to develop a well-planned approach to maintaining the plan on a sound and responsible financial course.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I consider that Bill C-19 is an imaginative and responsible approach to bringing the Canada Pension Plan into harmony with contemporary values and attitudes in Canadian society. I consider that the bill will bring the plan into line with the economic facts of Canadian life now and in the future. Furthermore, if the bill is passed into law it will allow the Canada Pension Plan to play a vital role in the new charter the government is writing for this country's aged, disabled, widows, widowers, orphans and those in need. I hope that
Canada Pension Plan
the bill will attract the overwhelming support of Canadians inside and outside parliament.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-19. At first blush, after reading the newspaper reports, I thought the act would give equal rights to male and female contributors. In fact the news release put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare, dated April 5, states:
Mr. Lalonde stated that a major purpose of the Bill, as indicated in the Throne Speech, is to establish equal treatment for male and female contributors and beneficiaries. This is in accordance with the agreement reached by the federal and provincial Ministers of Welfare at their meeting in Edmonton last February.
From reading the provisions of this bill it does not in fact give equal treatment. The news release is pure and simple window dressing.
When he spoke earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) went into detail on the provisions in the bill. He established beyond a doubt that there is not equality as far as male and female contributors are concerned. The bill does, however, give a survivor pension to widowers. This provision has been needed for a long time. There are many instances where a husband has been disabled and unable to work and the wife has been the breadwinner. There has been no provision for survivor benefits for the husband if she should pass on.
I welcome the removal of the earnings test for people between the ages of 65 and 70. I recall many instances in the practice of law where farmers, in particular, retired at age 65 and applied for Canada Pension Plan benefits. They either had wheat on hand, or would be receiving wheat board payments sometime in the future. They received the Canada Pension Plan benefits. When filing their income tax returns the following year they had to include grain sales and wheat board payments as part of their income. The result was they received letters shortly after filing their returns, stating they had been overpaid and asking for a refund of their Canada Pension Plan benefits. Basically this change is welcome.
There are other instances of people who retire at 65, people who had not earned that much during their lifetime. Their assets are such that they are not able to make ends meet. Even utilizing their Canada Pension Plan benefits they have to supplement their income. They find that, as a result of working to supplement their income, they lose part of their Canada Pension Plan benefits. This change in the act will do away with that inequity and I welcome it.
I also welcome the change in clause 8 which provides, and I quote:
-that income earned by a contributor but not actually received before his death be included as part of that contributor's contributory salary and wages.
Anyone involved in the handling of estates would have found this to be an inequity. It has created problems. Fortunately the government has seen fit, possibly because of representations, to make the necessary change in this act.
I also welcome the changes with regard to clauses applying to self-employed persons. The former requirement was that they had to earn at least one and one third of the

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
year's basic exemption to qualify as a contributor. The changes will enable a person who is self employed to contribute without complying with this provision.
The minister's news release of April 5 stated:
These changes will provide greater opportunity for people at lower income levels to participate in the Canada Pension Plan. In particular, increased numbers of farmers, fishermen and other self-employed persons will be enabled to improve their protection under the Plan.
I am interested in the reference to farmers. On March 19 of last year I submitted the following motion to this House:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Canada Pension Plan Act so as to allow farmers the option to make Canada Pension Plan contributions regardless of their net income.
There was a reason for submitting that motion for the consideration of the House. Farmers are in a difficult situation when it comes to their income. Their income is cyclical in nature. They are faced with the variations of price on the international market, with drought, with losses due to grasshopper infestation. Consequently their income fluctuates from year to year.
A farmer might have no taxable income for three years and then, for two years, he might have a substantial amount of income. During the three years in which he had little or no taxable income he is not able to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. In the two years in which he does receive a substantial amount of income he is able to contribute the maximum. He is, of course, able to average his income over a five year period and as a result he becomes taxable each year.
By becoming taxable each year he pays taxes based on the rates for each taxation year, but there is no provision for him to make CPP contributions. In other words while, in effect, his income has been taxable for those five years he can only make contributions for, say, two years. The result is that when he comes to collect payments on retirement the amount he is entitled to receive is reduced, despite the fact that during the over-all period he has possibly received substantially more income than a person earning wages over the same period.
I suggested, when I spoke on my motion, that these facts should be taken into consideration, and that the government should consider changes in the act allowing a farmer the option of making contributions to the plan regardless of his net income. The answer I received was to the effect that the plan was not actuarially sound. This came as a surprise to me. I had always assumed that the plan would be actuarially sound, in other words that it would pay its way.
I was told subsequently that, at the rate at which benefits were being paid out, the plan would go into the red some time in the 80's. Later I was advised that, as a result of the increase in the benefits payable last year, the plan would go into the red some time in the late 70's. It seems to me that if we do not examine the whole concept of this scheme we shall create a situation in which our children, and their children, will be paying for the benefits we ourselves will be receiving. I believe the plan must be actuarilly sound, and I suggest to the minister that he take

a hard look at it and give thought to arranging it in such a way that it will pay for itself without becoming a burden on our children.
There are one or two further comments I should like to make. At times there is undue delay in paying benefits-to widows, in particular. I have found that the regional offices are very efficient. I refer particularly to the office in Regina. When I was practising law I know that after a widow had gone there to complete the necessary documentation, the representatives of the administration locally would have the documents ready in a matter of a week or ten days. Naturally, having made an application and having been told the documentation was complete, the widow expected she would be receiving benefits within, say, a month or six weeks. This was the exception rather than the rule.
When I inquired about the delays the answer I received was that they arose in Ottawa-the red tape was there. I have known cases where a widow had to wait for as long as six months before receiving payments under the plan. And not only were payments delayed. In many instances, when the husband died later than the month of June, widows would receive five or six months of benefit payments in the following year, say, in January. Under the Income Tax Act these back payments are counted as income in the year in which they are received. Mr. Speaker, I have seen situations in which widows have paid income tax on as many as 18 months of benefits.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my comments on Bill C-190 I should like to echo the words of the hon. member who has just preceded me. Basically I am satisfied with the amendments, but I think that some matters which ought to have been included have been omitted, and that the government has not gone far enough in certain respects.
April 17, 1974

Basically I agree with the argument in favour of equality as between male and female contributors. The situation of the female contributor has been improved by placing her on the same basis as far as dependents are concerned. I think we shall probably be called upon to review the whole subject to arrive at a fair and equitable formula which will enable housewives to participate in this plan. I appreciate the difficulties. I have read the minister's paper with interest, and I hope he will be able to produce a sensible solution.
I have never been able to understand the section in the present act which, in effect, instituted a means test at the age of 65. It did not make sense to me that if you contributed to a plan which was the same as any other insurance plan, and which paid a universal benefit, your pension would be reduced by the amount of your outside earnings. So I am glad that the minister has seen fit to abolish what was, in effect, a means test at the age of 65.
The changes in the formula for the year's maximum pensionable earnings ceiling, which will result in a change in the formula for benefits will, I know, be accepted cheerfully by all contributors to the plan. It is probably long past the time when this plan should have been modernized and adapted to make it more compatible with the present d^v cost of living.
However, I should just like to reaffirm what other hon. members who have spoken before me said, that we are rapidly reaching the stage where we must be very careful in all this tinkering with, and adjusting of, the CPP. I feel we are rapidly getting to the point where we might get into the same kind of mess the Unemployment Insurance Act is in. That was a good act until the government decided to monkey around and to make out of it a trough for catching votes in 1971 by broadening its provisions. This made the plan no longer actuarially sound. I hope this will be a lesson to the minister, and that before we go on to make any more generous amendments to the act we will make sure that the present fund, and the payments to be made, will be sufficient to take care of the increased benefits that are being provided.
Having said that, and having complimented the minister for bringing in these amendments to the act, I am a little disappointed that certain other amendments have not been made. The Canada Pension Plan is basically a good plan; I do not think anyone would question that. I think it is part of our social planning. Individuals have been able to incorporate the plan into their own private arrangements, which I think is probably the only way a good many Canadians have been able to develop any kind of retirement pension for themselves.
As I say, it is a good plan, and I think most are happy with it, but there is one class of contributor that is, I think, discriminated against. I do not know whether it is because of the wording of the act or because of the way the act is being interpreted, but the chief complaints I get about the CPP come from those who have to retire from work before the age of 65. On applying for the pension, in many cases they are refused because they do not come within the definition of "disability" under the act. I think this is my chief complaint with the amendments we are studying today.
Canada Pension Plan
The definition of "disabled person" is contained in section 43(2) (a) of the act. That section reads as follows:
(2) For the purposes of this Act,
(a) a person shall be considered to be disabled only if he is determined in prescribed manner to be suffering from a severe and
prolonged mental or physical disability-
I do not know what is meant by "prescribed manner", but it seems to me that if a person has a medical certificate from a qualified medical practitioner to the effect that he is incapable of working, and that further work would be injurious to his health, then that should be sufficient to qualify him for the Canada pension to which he has contributed since the plan came into force. "Prescribed manner" would seem to me to indicate that an examination by a qualified medical practitioner should be sufficient.
The subsection goes on to provide:
-a disability is severe only if by reason thereof the person in respect of whom the determination is made is incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation-
If an applicant's doctor advises him that, by reason of heart failure or a lung condition, or any other physical disability, further work is injurious to his health and might in fact result in his death, then surely that should be sufficient to qualify him under the disability section of the act for a pension. In fact the subsection goes on to refer to illness or disability that is likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration, or is likely to result in death.
I had a case the other day of a woman who had had one coronary and two cardiac arrests. Her doctor certified that she should not even take part in any light work. Certainly if anything is likely to result in death, it is cardiac arrest. This woman applied for her pension but was refused. In fact she was told, even though she had her own doctor's certificate, to get another medical examination.
Therein, Mr. Speaker, lies the rub. I come from a small town, and like most small towns in this country there is a shortage of doctors. It is hard enough to get one medical examination done by your own physician, but when you are told that your own physician's report cannot be accepted and that you will have to get an outside opinion, you find it takes 60 to 90 days, if you are lucky, to get an appointment with another doctor. I do not know whether the officials of the Canada Pension Plan are hoping these people will die within the 90 days while they are waiting for the other opinion or what, but I sometimes wonder.
This situation is serious enough, but much to my surprise only last week I discovered that in the city of Moncton-I do not know whether this applies to other cities-there are no doctors either capable of rendering a professional opinion that is acceptable to the department or willing to examine patients sent to them by the Canada Pension Plan administration. I do not know whether this is because the fee that the CPP pays is not high enough, or whether the doctors there are simply fed up with this business of having their professional judgment questioned; but we now have the ridiculous situation where people with serious heart conditions, emphysema, or other serious disabilities are told there is no doctor in Moncton qualified or willing to give the CPP a satisfactory report, and so they have to go to Halifax or Saint John.
1530

April 17, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
When senior citizens who have had two or three heart attacks, and do not know how long they are going to last, are told that they have to take a bus, train or plane trip to Halifax, some 200 miles away from Moncton, to undergo a medical examination, the frustration and excitement are enough to knock them off.
I could not believe that this was the practice of the CPP, so I called the local office. The first reply to me was: "Oh no, this is only done in exceptional cases". When I asked what the exceptional cases were, I discovered they were heart cases and lung cases in particular. I consider these the two most common causes of physical disability necessitating early retirement from work, and I found the situation almost unbelievable.
I do not know whether this is a policy that has been laid down by the minister or his officials. People in the local office always say their hands are tied, that there is nothing they can do about it because it is determined by the Ottawa office. If that is the case I certainly feel that Section 43 should be revised in order to make clear what is meant by substantial or gainful occupation.
How disabled must you be before you are incapable of other work? Must you be a basket case, or bedridden? When a person has suffered three or four serious heart attacks, surely the fact that he is able to walk does not mean he is able to work, but this seems to be the interpretation placed on this section by officials administering the plan. These are the people who are suffering.
It is all right to say that there is an appeal provision, but anyone who has had any experience with the appeal procedure under the Canada Pension Plan will know that there is an initial three-month delay before you can get another medical opinion, and that medical opinion may not be accepted before the commencement of the appeal procedure. This is where the delay and frustration begin.
I remember an appeal a few years ago when it took 15 months from the time the application was put in until the appeal was disposed of finally. I cannot see the justice in decisions which delay the payment of benefits to persons who have been forced to pay into the plan because deductions were made from salary. Where is the justice in forcing these people to wait 15 months because officials of the department are not prepared to interpret the regulations as they should be interpreted, or because there is not sufficient staff to look after the applications?
Perhaps the wording of this section could be changed, or something could be made clear in respect of the interpretation of what is a substantial or gainful occupation. Is it fair to suggest that because an individual has been a carpenter, and cannot work with his disability, there is no reason why he cannot be a nightwatchman or perhaps run an elevator? This is one of the things that has bothered me. I use elevators quite a bit and, as many others, I am not happy having somebody operating an elevator who is so disabled this is the only type of job he can do. It does not make sense to tell a person who has had three or four heart attacks that he should take a job as a nightwatchman. I do not think we want a person who is apt to drop dead at any moment on that kind of a job.
I was happy to hear the minister refer to upcoming revisions. He talked about many things and I cannot find the exact reference, but he did say that amendments would cover several areas. There was reference to disability payments, but no reference to a definition of disability. The proposed bill makes reference to a clarification of the definition of disabled children, but does not make any reference to what is a disability, or what procedure must be followed for these people to qualify.
As I indicated earlier, I am in favour of the amendments and appreciate them as far as they go, but I hope the amendments the minister has promised to bring in will take into consideration this whole section I have mentioned. It may be possible to improve it by legislation, or it may be that all that is required is a direction to the officials regarding interpretation. When this goes to the committee I hope this will be one of the matters considered, so that this category of people now being discriminated against will be able to obtain the fair treatment they are entitled to as contributors under the act.
